Nine-Year-Old RefluXFS Linux Flaw Gives Local Users Root on Default RHEL Installs

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputer
2026-07-23 17 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

RefluXFS, a new Linux kernel flaw disclosed on July 22 and tracked as CVE-2026-64600, lets an unprivileged local user overwrite root-owned files on an XFS filesystem and gain persistent root access. Qualys said default installations of Red Hat Enterprise Linux and its derivatives, Fedora Server, and Amazon Linux can meet the conditions for exploitation. The company demonstrated the race

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] XFS reflink capability reconnaissance (RefluXFS CVE-2026-64600 pre-exploit) · [LLM] RefluXFS CVE-2026-64600 exposure: reflink-XFS hosts on unpatched kernels · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

XFS reflink capability reconnaissance (RefluXFS CVE-2026-64600 pre-exploit) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts unprivileged users enumerating whether a mounted XFS volume was created with reflink=1 — the exploit precondition the Qualys advisory checks with 'xfs_info / | grep reflink='. Article-specific because RefluXFS only fires on reflink-enabled XFS, so this recon directly precedes exploitation. Rationale: Anchors on the exact advisory command 'xfs_info / | grep reflink=' and the reflink= token — a filesystem-feature check that unprivileged users almost never run and that is mandatory before RefluXFS can be attempted. Cross-checked against Qualys blog and oss-security post which both cite this precondition. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/07/22/14 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/linux/new-refluxfs-linux-flaw-lets-attackers-gain-root-privileges/
ATT&CKT1082 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Storage/sysadmin auditing XFS features during capacity planning
  • Configuration-management tools (Ansible/Puppet facts) invoking xfs_info
  • Backup software checking reflink support before dedup
  • Container-image build pipelines probing the filesystem
  • Monitoring agents inventorying mount options
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","python3","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","veeam") and AccountName !in~ ("ansible","backup","monitoring")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the invoking account and whether it is an untrusted/low-privilege principal (CI runner, service account, interactive shell on a multi-tenant host); confirm the host runs reflink=1 XFS and check its patch date against RHSA-2026:39179/39180/39494. Step 2 (contain): If the account is untrusted and the host is unpatched, isolate the host or suspend the session/CI job; verify no follow-on root shell appeared. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same account/host for chsh execution, FICLONE-heavy write loops, and any non-root process yielding a uid-0 shell within seconds.

| where AccountName != "root" and AccountName !endswith "$"
| where AccountName !in~ ("system","_apt")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

chsh executed by unprivileged user to reset RefluXFS unshared-block precondition AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unprivileged invocations of chsh, which the Qualys advisory names as the trick an attacker uses to reset a target file to the 'unshared block' state required to fire the RefluXFS race. chsh is rarely run interactively, making it a specific, low-noise precursor signal for CVE-2026-64600. Rationale: The advisory explicitly states an unprivileged user can reset the unshared-block condition 'by running chsh' — a named, uncommon binary tied directly to the exploit workflow, giving higher fidelity than generic setuid abuse. Corroborated by Qualys blog and The Hacker News body. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nine-year-old-refluxfs-linux-flaw-gives.html

Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine if the account is a real interactive user changing shells vs. an untrusted principal on a reflink=1 XFS host; check for xfs_info recon or a subsequent uid-0 shell from the same session within minutes. Step 2 (contain): If untrusted and the host is unpatched for CVE-2026-64600, suspend the session and isolate the host; snapshot /etc/passwd and all setuid-root binary hashes for later comparison. Step 3 (hunt): Look for tight-loop writers against cloned scratch files and any root logon or setuid-binary content drift on the host over the next hours.

Root shell spawned by non-root process without sudo/su (RefluXFS LPE outcome) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the privilege-transition fingerprint of a local root exploit: a shell running as uid 0 whose parent process ran as a non-root user and was NOT launched via a legitimate elevation path (sudo/su/pkexec/sshd/login). RefluXFS grants root by overwriting a setuid-root binary or /etc/passwd, so the resulting root shell appears without an authorized elevation event. Rationale: Uses the process-tree uid transition (non-root parent -> uid-0 shell) that any local root exploit including RefluXFS produces, and neutralises the dominant FP source by excluding legitimate elevation binaries (sudo/su/pkexec/sshd). The article states 'local users' reliably 'gain root' via a modified setuid-root binary, which yields exactly this signature. Corroborated by Qualys and oss-security. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/07/22/14
ATT&CKT1068 T1548.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Setuid helper tools (e.g. custom sudo-like wrappers) not in the exclusion list
  • Container runtimes/entrypoints launching root shells outside systemd
  • CI agents that execute steps as root without sudo
  • Monitoring/backup agents spawning root maintenance shells
  • Legacy init scripts invoking shells as root
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("containerd-shim","runc","dockerd","podman","gitlab-runner","buildkitd","veeam","backup")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the parent process and its command line — is it a known setuid helper or an anomalous binary? Confirm whether the host is reflink=1 XFS and unpatched for CVE-2026-64600, and whether the parent account is untrusted. Step 2 (contain): If unexplained, kill the root shell, isolate the host, and preserve /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and setuid-root binary hashes; force a reboot to a verified fixed kernel (the exploit persists across reboots). Step 3 (hunt): Compare all setuid-root binary content hashes against a known-good gold image (metadata is untouched, so trust only content), and review the account's prior chsh/xfs_info activity.

Anomalous direct root logon after RefluXFS /etc/passwd password strip AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts successful interactive/remote root logons on Linux hosts — the payoff of the RefluXFS PoC, which strips the root password by overwriting /etc/passwd so an attacker can authenticate as root directly. On hardened multi-tenant/CI hosts where direct root login is normally disabled, any such success is a high-value signal. Rationale: Targets the article's demonstrated outcome — 'The published demo strips the root password on a default RHEL 10.2 box' — by surfacing direct root authentication that bypasses sudo/su, using a 30-day per-host baseline anti-join to flag first-seen root logons. Corroborated by Qualys and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/linux/new-refluxfs-linux-flaw-lets-attackers-gain-root-privileges/
ATT&CKT1078.003 T1556.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate break-glass root login by an on-call admin
  • New host provisioning where root login is briefly enabled
  • Automation/orchestration authenticating as root over SSH with keys
  • Console/KVM root login during maintenance
  • A host that only recently began forwarding logon telemetry (empty baseline)
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("10.0.0.5","10.0.0.6") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "break-glass"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether direct root login is policy-permitted on this host; check the source IP, whether MFA/key auth was used, and whether /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow shows a missing root hash. Correlate with prior xfs_info/chsh activity or a non-root->uid-0 shell on the same host. Step 2 (contain): If unauthorized, kill the root session, rotate root/user credentials and SSH keys, restore /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow from a trusted backup, and patch+reboot to a fixed kernel. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate persistence — modified setuid-root binaries (content-hash drift with unchanged timestamps), new SSH authorized_keys, and cron/systemd units added under root.

RefluXFS CVE-2026-64600 exposure: reflink-XFS hosts on unpatched kernels AIReconnaissance High
Exposure hunt that inventories hosts flagged vulnerable to CVE-2026-64600 so patch-and-reboot can be prioritised on multi-tenant/CI systems per the Qualys guidance. Directly actionable because the only remediation is a fixed kernel plus reboot, and installing the package does not replace the running kernel. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-64600) against vulnerability-inventory tables to enumerate exposed hosts, matching the advisory's 'patch exposed and multi-tenant systems first' guidance. Confirmed against Red Hat's tracker (RHSA-2026:39179/39180/39494) and Qualys advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7145752 • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already rebooted onto a fixed kernel but scanner still reports the installed-but-inactive vulnerable package until next scan
  • RHEL 7 hosts mis-flagged despite predating XFS reflink support
  • XFS volumes without reflink=1 flagged by a version-only check (not exploitable)
  • Scanner lag showing stale severity after errata applied
  • Air-gapped hosts where package metadata is out of date
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each flagged host, verify the running kernel with 'uname -r' against the fixed build (installing the errata does not replace the in-memory kernel) and check whether root XFS actually has reflink=1. Step 2 (contain): Prioritise multi-tenant, CI, and internet-facing hosts; apply the vendor errata (RHSA-2026:39179/39180 for RHEL 8, RHSA-2026:39494 for RHEL 10) and schedule a reboot, since there is no runtime mitigation. Step 3 (hunt): On any host that stayed unpatched, review for xfs_info/chsh precursors and non-root->root shell transitions to rule out exploitation before patching.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'

    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-64600")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Attackers Weaponize GitHub Actions Runners to Target cPanel and WHM Servers

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 18 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have shed light on a large-scale campaign that has turned compromised GitHub repositories into distributed attack infrastructure designed to target cPanel and WebHost Manager (WHM) instances. The activity involves malicious Packagist development versions spanning 10 packages associated with a legitimate PHP and DevOps developer, dinushchathurya, between July 12 and 13,

CVEsCVE-2026-41940
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1059.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1204.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566
Domainsf5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba606085d.dnshook.site
IPs43.228.157.68

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious Packagist install: compromised dinushchathurya/* PHP packages · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Egress to cPanel/WHM campaign C2 43.228.157.68 (Linux payload download + result POST) · [LLM] DNSHook C2/exfil beacon to *.dnshook.site (campaign GUID f5b0b742) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Server-side secret harvest fan-out (AWS/SSH/Git/DB/Stripe) by single process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Egress to cPanel/WHM campaign C2 43.228.157.68 (Linux payload download + result POST) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host (self-hosted GitHub Actions runner, build server, or cPanel host) making a network connection to the campaign C2 at 43.228.157.68, which serves the architecture-specific Linux scanning/exploitation payload and receives HTTP POST exfil of harvested secrets. Article-specific because the IP is the single C2 for both payload delivery and result upload. Rationale: Pivots on the exact campaign C2 IP 43.228.157.68 named by Socket/THN as both payload host and exfil sink. IP is cited only by the original reporting (not independently corroborated), hence Medium confidence; the CVE and DNSHook identifier around it are corroborated. Cross-checked against: • https://success.trendmicro.com/en-US/solution/KA-0023294 • https://labs.watchtowr.com/the-internet-is-falling-down-falling-down-falling-down-cpanel-whm-authentication-bypass-cve-2026-41940/ • https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-41940
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security team intentionally sandbox-detonating the payload and reaching the C2
  • Threat-intel/scanning platform (Shodan/Censys style) that happens to share the /24 hosting the IP
  • Shared hosting neighbor if the IP is later reassigned to a benign tenant
  • Proxy/NAT egress device logging the connection on behalf of an internal host (source attribution ambiguity)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and host role (self-hosted runner? build server? cPanel host?) via InitiatingProcessCommandLine; confirm direction/bytes (large POST = exfil). 2) Contain: block 43.228.157.68 at egress firewall, isolate the host, and freeze/rotate any secrets reachable from it (AWS keys, GitHub/GitLab tokens, SSH keys, DB/Stripe/SendGrid creds). 3) Hunt: search the same host and org for DNS to dnshook.site, composer installs of dinushchathurya/* packages, and .github/workflows files containing the DNSHook GUID f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "43.228.157.68"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "43.228.157.68"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6f3b2e2a-1c4d-4c8e-9a1b-2f7e5d9c1a01

  - attack.t1071.001

  category: network_connection
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationIp: '43.228.157.68'
  condition: selection

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="43.228.157.68"
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemotePort], function=count())
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action, bytes

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="43.228.157.68" by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app host | `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")` | sort - lastTime

DNSHook C2/exfil beacon to *.dnshook.site (campaign GUID f5b0b742) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS/URL resolution to the DNSHook exfiltration channel used across the ~6,100-workflow campaign, keyed on the dnshook.site parent domain and the unique campaign identifier f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d. Any resolution is high-fidelity — the GUID subdomain is globally unique to this operation. Rationale: Uses the corroborated DNSHook identifier f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d and the dnshook.site parent domain; a globally-unique GUID subdomain makes any resolution effectively zero-FP. Datadog/CloudWatch left empty as the provided schemas expose no clean DNS-query field for those sources. Cross-checked against: • https://healsecurity.com/compromised-github-action-exfiltrates-workflow-credentials-to-attacker-domain/ • https://gbhackers.com/compromised-github-action/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Passive-DNS / threat-intel enrichment tools resolving the IOC domain for research
  • Sandbox detonation of a captured workflow inside your environment
  • Security researcher manually curling the domain during analysis
  • DNS sinkhole appliance that itself resolves the domain before blackholing
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the process that triggered the lookup (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName); a runner or CI agent resolving this is credential exfil in progress. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block *.dnshook.site at DNS egress, isolate the host, and immediately rotate every secret the host could access (cloud keys, VCS tokens, SSH, DB, payment API keys). 3) Hunt: correlate to connections to 43.228.157.68 and to any local composer installs of dinushchathurya/* or workflow files carrying the campaign GUID.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "dnshook.site" or RemoteUrl contains "f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "dnshook.site"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious Packagist install: compromised dinushchathurya/* PHP packages AIDelivery High
Hunts build/dev hosts running composer against any of the ten compromised dinushchathurya packages whose July 12-13 2026 dev versions carry the malicious GitHub Actions workflows. Article-specific because it keys on the exact compromised maintainer namespace, not generic composer usage. Rationale: Keys on the exact compromised namespace 'dinushchathurya/' (10 packages incl. uk-post-code, uk-mobile-number-validator, websmslk) confirmed by Socket and the CVE-2026-41940 coverage; scoping to the maintainer name keeps FPs to legitimate re-installs of these specific libraries only. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/attackers-weaponize-github-actions.html • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/cve-2026-41940-explained-cpanel-whm-authentication-bypass-hit-1-5m-servers
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately using a clean (pre-July-12) pinned version of one of these libraries
  • CI cache-warming or mirror-sync jobs that reference the package name without pulling the malicious dev version
  • Security team reproducing the supply-chain issue in a lab
  • Composer audit/SCA tooling echoing the package name in its own command line
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("require","update","install","remove") and not (ProcessCommandLine has "--dry-run")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolved version — malicious dev versions synced July 12-13 2026; inspect the pulled vendor/dinushchathurya/*/.github/workflows tree for YAML containing the GUID f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d. 2) Contain: purge the composer cache and vendor dir, pin to a known-good version, and block outbound to 43.228.157.68 / dnshook.site from build infra. 3) Hunt: enumerate all repos/runners that consumed the package, review GitHub Actions run history for runner egress to the C2, and rotate any secrets exposed to those workflows.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "dinushchathurya/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "dinushchathurya/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Install of Compromised dinushchathurya Packagist Package
id: 8c1a4f6b-3d92-4a7e-b5f0-9e2c7a1d4c03
description: Detects composer/PHP command line referencing the compromised dinushchathurya package namespace carrying malicious GitHub Actions workflows.

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:
  - attack.initial_access

logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains: 'dinushchathurya/'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:*dinushchathurya/*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/dinushchathurya\//i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*dinushchathurya/*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process host | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*dinushchathurya/*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process host | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | sort - lastTime
Server-side secret harvest fan-out (AWS/SSH/Git/DB/Stripe) by single process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single process on a server or runner touching multiple distinct credential stores in one burst — the exact secret classes the campaign payload harvests before POSTing to C2 (AWS creds, GitHub/GitLab tokens, SSH keys, DB configs, Stripe/SendGrid/Mailgun keys). Article-specific via the enumerated secret-file set; catches the credential-theft stage independent of the C2 IOCs. Rationale: Enumerates the precise secret-file set matching the article's harvested-data list (AWS credentials, GitHub/GitLab tokens, SSH material, DB info, Stripe/SendGrid/Mailgun keys); requiring >=4 distinct stores touched by one process separates the stealer sweep from a service reading its own single config. Sigma omitted (aggregation/threshold, not single-event); Datadog/CloudWatch omitted as the provided schemas lack file-read fields. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/attackers-weaponize-github-actions.html • https://gbhackers.com/compromised-github-action/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/sync agents (restic, borg, rsync, tar) sweeping home directories
  • A legitimate CI job that legitimately reads .aws/credentials + .npmrc + .git-credentials during a build
  • Configuration-management runs (Ansible/Chef) templating multiple dotfiles
  • Developer environment bootstrap scripts (dotfile installers) touching many config files at once
  • Endpoint DLP or secret-scanning tools that themselves open credential files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("restic","borg","rsync","tar","ansible","veeam","duplicity")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the fan-out process image and command line — an unsigned/ephemeral ELF or a curl/bash child of the CI runner reading 4+ secret stores is malicious; a known backup binary is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host and immediately rotate every credential the process could have read (cloud keys, VCS tokens, SSH keys, DB creds, Stripe/SendGrid/Mailgun API keys). 3) Hunt: check the same host for subsequent egress to 43.228.157.68 or dnshook.site (the exfil POST) and pivot org-wide on that process hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has_any (".aws/credentials", "/.ssh/id_rsa", "/.ssh/id_ed25519", ".git-credentials", ".npmrc", ".netrc", ".my.cnf", "gh/hosts.yml") or FileName endswith ".env"
| summarize DistinctSecrets = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFiles = make_set(FolderPath, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where DistinctSecrets >= 4
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (".aws/credentials", ".ssh/id_rsa", ".ssh/id_ed25519", ".git-credentials", ".npmrc", ".netrc", ".my.cnf", "gh/hosts.yml", ".env")
| summarize DistinctSecrets = dcount(TargetFilePath), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId
| where DistinctSecrets >= 4
| order by FirstSeen desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/(\.aws\/credentials|\.ssh\/id_(rsa|ed25519)|\.git-credentials|\.npmrc|\.netrc|\.my\.cnf|gh\/hosts\.yml|\.env)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true))
| _count >= 4
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinct_secrets values(Filesystem.file_path) as files min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*/.aws/credentials" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/id_rsa" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/id_ed25519" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.git-credentials" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.npmrc" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.netrc" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.my.cnf" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.env") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id host | `drop_dm_object_name("Filesystem")` | where distinct_secrets>=4 | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinct_secrets values(Filesystem.file_path) as files min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*/.aws/credentials" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/id_rsa" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/id_ed25519" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.git-credentials" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.npmrc" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.netrc" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.my.cnf" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.env") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id host | `drop_dm_object_name("Filesystem")` | where distinct_secrets>=4 | sort - firstTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176

    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-41940")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-41940")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel

Cisco Talos
2026-07-23 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Chaos ransomware group uses new malware "msaRAT" that hijacks browsers. The malware doesn't communicate directly with C2 but connects through the browser. It enables arbitrary command execution while hiding the attacker's IP from victims via WebRTC over TURN.

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1486
Domainsis-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev
IPs172.86.126.18
