Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] msaRAT delivery: curl.exe fetching fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData over HTTP
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] msaRAT msiexec executing update_ms.msi (fake Windows update custom action)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] msaRAT CDP abuse: headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging port spawned by non-browser parent · [LLM] msaRAT C2 network IOC: connection to 172.86.126.18 or is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
msaRAT delivery: curl.exe fetching fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData over HTTP AIDelivery High
Hunts the Chaos ransomware pre-ransom delivery step where curl.exe downloads update_ms.msi from attacker IP 172.86.126.18 (plain HTTP on port 443) into C:\programdata\. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact filename, ProgramData sink, and hardcoded C2 IP. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim curl command from the article (update_ms.msi, hardcoded 172.86.126.18, ProgramData sink) — the triple combination is essentially unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199 • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/new-chaos-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using curl to stage a genuine .msi in ProgramData for software deployment
  • Internal software-distribution tooling pulling installers over HTTP to a ProgramData staging folder
  • Security researcher / detection-lab replaying the sample
  • RMM agent using curl to fetch an update package into ProgramData
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible.exe","chocolatey.exe","choco.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "172.86.126.18")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the curl invocation targeted 172.86.126.18 or the literal update_ms.msi filename and that the destination is C:\programdata\; pull the parent process and user. 2. Contain: network-isolate the host, block 172.86.126.18 at the perimeter, and quarantine C:\programdata\update_ms.msi before it is executed by msiexec. 3. Hunt: pivot to msiexec execution of that MSI, headless Chrome/Edge launches with --remote-debugging-port, and outbound traffic to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev across the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update_ms.msi", "172.86.126.18")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "programdata"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "curl.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("update_ms.msi", "172.86.126.18")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "programdata"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: msaRAT Delivery via curl Downloading Fake Windows Update MSI to ProgramData
id: 6c2f4b1a-9d3e-4a77-8f2b-11a2c9d4e5f0
description: Detects Chaos ransomware msaRAT delivery where curl.exe downloads update_ms.msi from attacker IP 172.86.126.18 into ProgramData
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1218.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\curl.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'update_ms.msi'
      - '172.86.126.18'
  location:
    CommandLine|contains: 'programdata'
  condition: selection and location
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\curl.exe OR *\\Curl.exe OR *\\CURL.EXE) (@CommandLine:*update_ms.msi* OR @CommandLine:*172.86.126.18*) @CommandLine:*programdata*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/curl\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(update_ms\.msi|172\.86\.126\.18)/i
| CommandLine=/programdata/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=curl.exe (Processes.process="*update_ms.msi*" OR Processes.process="*172.86.126.18*") Processes.process="*programdata*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=curl.exe (Processes.process="*update_ms.msi*" OR Processes.process="*172.86.126.18*") Processes.process="*programdata*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
msaRAT msiexec executing update_ms.msi (fake Windows update custom action) AIInstallation High
Hunts the second delivery stage: msiexec.exe executing the Chaos-dropped update_ms.msi whose custom action CA_Run_EA2AEBC3 reflectively loads lib.dll (msaRAT) into memory. Article-specific via the exact MSI filename. Rationale: The MSI filename update_ms.msi is a verbatim article IOC; msiexec running it from ProgramData is the reflective-load launcher for lib.dll (msaRAT). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor MSI happening to be staged in ProgramData (broad hunting clause only)
  • Patch-management tool invoking msiexec against a ProgramData-cached installer
  • Detection-lab replay of the sample
  • Third-party updater masquerading its own installer in ProgramData
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi"
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm msiexec ran update_ms.msi and inspect the MSI's Binary table / custom action (CA_Run_*) and file metadata spoofing Microsoft. 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill any child processes, and capture memory before reboot to recover the in-memory lib.dll (msaRAT). 3. Hunt: look for the RUN export being invoked, headless browser launches with CDP flags, and workers.dev / Twilio TURN egress to confirm C2 establishment.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or (ProcessCommandLine has @"\programdata\" and ProcessCommandLine has ".msi")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "msiexec.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or (TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\programdata\" and TargetProcessCommandLine has ".msi")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT CDP abuse: headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging port spawned by non-browser parent AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts msaRAT's core 'living off the browser' behaviour — it launches Chrome or Edge in headless mode with the CDP remote-debugging port enabled to drive a covert WebRTC C2. Detects browsers started with --headless/--remote-debugging-port by a parent that is not a browser or explorer. Rationale: The article states msaRAT launches Chrome/Edge headless via CreateProcessW with the remote-debugging port enabled to drive CDP; a browser started with these flags by a non-browser parent is a high-fidelity signal of programmatic browser hijack. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chaes-malware-now-uses-google-chrome-devtools-protocol-to-steal-data/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium automation frameworks launching headless Chrome for testing
  • CI/CD build agents rendering pages via headless Chrome
  • PDF-generation or web-scraping services spawning headless browsers
  • Developer tooling that opens Chrome with --remote-debugging-port for debugging
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe", "python.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cypress.exe", "chromedriver.exe", "selenium.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the parent process that spawned the headless browser and the remote-debugging port; benign automation parents (node.exe from a known project) differ sharply from msiexec/rundll32/unknown. 2. Contain: if the parent is unexpected, isolate the host and terminate the browser + parent process tree, then capture memory for the in-memory msaRAT. 3. Hunt: correlate with the CDP JSON endpoint (/json/list/) on localhost, WebRTC/TURN egress to global.turn.twilio.com, and connections to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port", "--headless")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe", "chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "msedgewebview2.exe", "userinit.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port", "--headless")
| where not(ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe", "chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "msedgewebview2.exe", "userinit.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: msaRAT Headless Browser with Remote Debugging Port Spawned by Non-Browser Parent
id: 8b3d5e2a-1c7f-4d99-a2b6-33c9f1e8d0a4
description: Detects Chrome/Edge launched headless with CDP remote-debugging port by a non-browser parent, as used by Chaos ransomware msaRAT for covert browser-fronted C2
references:

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/--(remote-debugging-port|headless)/i
| NOT (ParentBaseFileName=/(explorer|chrome|msedge|msedgewebview2|userinit)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

msaRAT C2 network IOC: connection to 172.86.126.18 or is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network contact with the hardcoded Chaos/msaRAT infrastructure — the delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the Cloudflare Workers signaling endpoint is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev used for SDP/ICE exchange. Pure IOC pivot corroborated by Talos. Rationale: Both the delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the Cloudflare Workers signaling domain are verbatim, campaign-unique IOCs from the Talos article; direct network matches are the highest-fidelity possible pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate host also using an unrelated *.workers.dev service (mitigated by the exact subdomain match)
  • Threat-intel sandbox / detonation VM deliberately contacting the IOC
  • Security scanner probing the attacker IP
  • Proxy log replay from an IR investigation
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the source host and the initiating process (a browser process for the workers.dev signaling, or curl/msiexec for the delivery IP). 2. Contain: block 172.86.126.18 and is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev at the firewall/proxy and network-isolate the source host. 3. Hunt: on the host, look back for the curl download of update_ms.msi, msiexec execution, headless browser launch with CDP flags, RMM tooling, and outbound Twilio TURN (global.turn.twilio.com) traffic indicating the WebRTC DataChannel is live.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18" or RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "172.86.126.18" or DestinationHostName =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or RequestURL has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT dropper: msiexec running 'update_ms.msi' Windows-Update decoy loading lib.dll AIInstallation High
Hunts the Chaos-group msaRAT installer stage where an MSI masquerading as a Windows update (update_ms.msi) is executed by msiexec.exe and reflectively loads the Rust backdoor lib.dll (export 'RUN') into memory. Anchored on the exact Talos-documented file names rather than generic MSI abuse. Rationale: Uses the concrete Talos IOC file name 'update_ms.msi' (the Windows-update decoy MSI that loads lib.dll) rather than generic msiexec abuse, making it near-zero-FP. Corroborated by the Cisco Talos report mirrored on malware.news which names the MSI and the lib.dll 'RUN' export. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/new-chaos-ransomware/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal software-packaging team happens to name a real MSI 'update_ms.msi' during patch testing
  • A third-party updater that bundles its payload as update_ms.msi (rare)
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in a monitored sandbox that ships telemetry to the same tenant
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","services.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Windows\\CCM") // exclude SCCM-driven installs
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the msiexec parent chain and the SHA256 of update_ms.msi; confirm whether it is Microsoft-signed and where it was downloaded from (check DeviceFileEvents FileOriginUrl / 172.86.126.18). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill msiexec/child browser processes, and quarantine update_ms.msi + any lib.dll dropped under Temp/AppData/ProgramData. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a headless Chrome/Edge launch with --remote-debugging (UC2) and outbound to *.ols-img-12.workers.dev (UC3) within minutes of the install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "update_ms.msi"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=msiexec.exe (Processes.process="*update_ms.msi*" OR Processes.process="*update_ms*\.msi*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Headless Chrome/Edge launched with Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) remote debugging enabled AIExploitation High
Detects msaRAT hijacking a browser by spawning chrome.exe or msedge.exe in headless mode (--headless) with the remote debugging interface enabled (--remote-debugging-port / --remote-debugging-pipe) so the RAT can drive it over CDP and inject its JavaScript C2 channel. This flag combination on a user endpoint is the core browser-hijack signature. Rationale: The article states msaRAT 'launches the browser in headless mode' and 'enables the browser's remote debugging interface and connects to it via CDP' — the --headless + --remote-debugging flag pair is the literal execution artifact of that behaviour. Talos confirms CDP control over the headless session. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1564.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright automated UI test rigs launching headless Chrome with a debug port
  • Headless Chrome used for server-side PDF/screenshot rendering by an internal app
  • CI/CD runners performing browser-based end-to-end tests
  • RPA tooling (e.g. UiPath) driving a headless browser
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe","playwright.exe","cypress.exe","code.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Jenkins\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\actions-runner\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process — legitimate uses are parented by node.exe/python/chromedriver/CI agents; msaRAT's browser is parented by an anomalous host (msiexec/rundll32/unknown). Note the --user-data-dir and debugging port. 2) Contain: if the parent is not sanctioned automation, isolate the host and terminate the browser + parent. 3) Hunt: correlate to a loopback CDP session (127.0.0.1:9222, /json/list/) and outbound to *.ols-img-12.workers.dev / turn.twilio.com from the same browser PID (UC3/UC4), and check for update_ms.msi (UC1).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port" or ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-pipe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe","code.exe","selenium-manager.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--headless"
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port" or CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-pipe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "\\node.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\chromedriver.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\msedgedriver.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser beaconing to msaRAT Cloudflare Workers signaling endpoint / hardcoded staging IP AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the msaRAT C2 signaling channel where the hijacked browser contacts the Cloudflare Workers endpoint is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev to obtain WebRTC connection info, and/or the hardcoded staging host 172.86.126.18 used to deliver the MSI. Anchored on the exact Talos/BleepingComputer network IOCs. Rationale: Uses the two hardest network IOCs in the article/Talos report: the exact Cloudflare Workers host is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev (WebRTC signaling relay) and staging IP 172.86.126.18 (MSI download). The full-domain match keeps FPs near zero while the .ols-img-12 subdomain wildcard catches sibling workers.dev subdomains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/new-chaos-ransomware/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199

  • A benign in-house app legitimately deployed on the same *.ols-img-12.workers.dev tenant (unlikely — this is attacker-controlled)
  • Threat-intel/sandbox appliances resolving the IOC domain for enrichment
  • Security proxies pre-fetching the domain for categorization
  • An analyst manually browsing to the IOC during investigation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") // exclude Defender enrichment lookups
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is a browser (chrome/msedge) and whether that browser instance was launched headless with CDP (UC2); capture RemoteIP/RemotePort and full workers.dev host. 2) Contain: block ols-img-12.workers.dev and 172.86.126.18 at egress/DNS, isolate the host, kill the browser + parent. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host/user for update_ms.msi (UC1) and Twilio TURN traffic (UC4); sweep the org for any other host resolving *.ols-img-12.workers.dev.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has "ols-img-12.workers.dev") or (RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true

(ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == "172.86.126.18" or DstHostname has "ols-img-12.workers.dev" | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Indicator="net-ioc")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hijacked browser routing C2 over WebRTC via Twilio TURN relay (msaRAT) AICommand & Control Medium
Correlates a headless/CDP browser launch with outbound WebRTC signaling to Twilio TURN (global.turn.twilio.com) and Google STUN (stun2.l.google.com) — the msaRAT design that omits ICE candidates to force all C2 traffic through the TURN relay, hiding the attacker's real server. The join to the headless-browser launch removes benign WebRTC noise. Rationale: The article states C2 is 'relayed through Twilio TURN servers' with ICE candidates omitted so all traffic is forced through TURN; Talos names global.turn.twilio.com and stun2.l.google.com. Twilio TURN/Google STUN alone are benign WebRTC, so the detection joins them to a headless+CDP browser launch (msaRAT-specific) to raise fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1572 T1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebRTC apps using Twilio TURN (video conferencing, customer-support widgets) running in a real (non-headless) browser tab
  • Google Meet / WebRTC test pages hitting stun2.l.google.com from an interactive browser
  • Developer testing a WebRTC app headlessly via Playwright/Selenium (parent will be a dev tool)
  • Browser prefetch/telemetry probing STUN reachability
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--type=renderer" // TURN/STUN from the msaRAT control context, not a normal renderer tab
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the browser instance contacting TURN/STUN is the same headless+CDP process (join hit) and NOT a user-facing tab; inspect its --user-data-dir and parent. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the browser + parent, and block the msaRAT signaling host ols-img-12.workers.dev at egress (TURN/STUN cannot be blanket-blocked without breaking conferencing). 3) Hunt: pull update_ms.msi/lib.dll (UC1), Workers signaling (UC3), and check for RMM tooling + phishing origin per the Chaos IR pattern (email/voice phishing → RMM install).
let CDPBrowsers = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port" or ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-pipe"
    | project DeviceId, LaunchTime = Timestamp, BrowserCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("global.turn.twilio.com","turn.twilio.com","stun2.l.google.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| join kind=inner CDPBrowsers on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (LaunchTime .. LaunchTime + 1h)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, LaunchTime, BrowserCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let CDPBrowsers = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where (NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe")
    | where CommandLine has "--headless" and (CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port" or CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-pipe")
    | project Computer, LaunchTime = TimeGenerated;
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("turn.twilio.com","stun2.l.google.com")
| join kind=inner (CDPBrowsers | project DvcHostname = Computer, LaunchTime) on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (LaunchTime .. LaunchTime + 1h)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, LaunchTime
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Check Point Patches Exploited SmartConsole Flaw Allowing Full Admin Access

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputer
2026-07-23 18 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Check Point has released security updates to address multiple vulnerabilities impacting Security Management and Multi-Domain Management (MDSM) products, including a critical flaw that has come under active exploitation in the wild. The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-16232 (CVSS score: 9.3), is an authentication bypass affecting the Check Point SmartConsole login process that allows an

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Check Point Management Server contacted by CVE-2026-16232 exploitation IOC IPs · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2026-16232 SmartConsole auth-bypass: admin login/token from external source · [LLM] CVE-2026-62145 Gaia Portal read-only user executing commands as root · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] New Check Point administrator account created from external / IOC source (post-compromise persistence) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Check Point Management run-script / exec-command on Security Gateway (CVE-2026-62144) · [LLM] Post-exploitation Check Point firewall policy / rule modification from campaign source · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Check Point Management Server contacted by CVE-2026-16232 exploitation IOC IPs AIDelivery Medium
Hunts network telemetry for the six attacker source IPs Check Point published for the actively-exploited SmartConsole authentication-bypass campaign (CVE-2026-16232 / CVE-2026-62144). Any Management Server or managed device communicating with these IPs is a direct campaign indicator. Rationale: Uses the six exact IOC IPs Check Point disclosed for the actively-exploited campaign; a Management Server (which should only talk to trusted admin subnets) contacting any of these is high-fidelity. Corroborated against Check Point sk185152 and CISA KEV listing. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/check-point-patches-exploited.html • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/22/cisa-adds-two-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk185152/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-16232-critical-check-point-smartconsole-authentication-bypass-exploited-in-the-wild/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanning/enrichment appliance (e.g. a TIP or honeypot) that deliberately reaches out to reported IOC IPs
  • Shared cloud/hosting IP that later gets reassigned to a legitimate SaaS the org uses
  • Security researcher or red-team box in the org that reuses one of the listed ranges
  • Passive DNS / netflow collector logging the IP without an actual session
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which internal asset communicated with the IOC IP and whether it is the Check Point Management Server or a managed gateway; pull the full session (ports, bytes, direction) and the DeviceAction. 2) Contain: block the IOC IPs at perimeter, and if the Management Server is internet-exposed, immediately restrict Trusted Clients to trusted subnets and place management behind a firewall per Check Point guidance. 3) Hunt: review SmartConsole admin login/audit records around the connection time for token issuance, run-script/exec-command activity, and any new administrator objects or policy installs.

CVE-2026-16232 SmartConsole auth-bypass: admin login/token from external source AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Check Point management audit telemetry for SmartConsole administrator authentication/token issuance originating from a public (non-RFC1918) source IP — the exact precondition (Management exposed without Trusted-Client IP restriction) that CVE-2026-16232 abuses to obtain a login token with full admin privileges. Rationale: Keys on Check Point SmartConsole/cpm admin authentication events from a non-private source IP, which is the precise 'Management exposed without Trusted-Client restriction' condition the article says the auth bypass requires. Defender/Falcon left empty because SmartConsole auth is Check Point management-plane telemetry not present in EDR. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/check-point-patches-exploited.html • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-16232-critical-check-point-smartconsole-authentication-bypass-exploited-in-the-wild/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/check-point-patches-smartconsole-zero-day-exploited-in-attacks/
ATT&CKT1190 T1548 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator connecting SmartConsole over the internet from a home/branch IP when management is (mis)configured as internet-facing
  • MSP/reseller managing the tenant from their own public egress IP
  • VPN split-tunnel that presents the admin's public IP to the management server
  • NAT gateway rewriting internal admin traffic to a public address
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("known-remote-admin-account") // maintain an allowlist of admins legitimately permitted to connect from public IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceIP and admin account, geolocate the IP, and confirm whether that admin has ever legitimately connected from outside the trusted subnets; compare against the published IOC list. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, disable/rotate that administrator's credentials and API keys, enforce Trusted-Client IP restriction, and firewall the management interface. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same session for run-script/exec-command, policy installations, and administrator-object creation to determine post-auth impact.
CommonSecurityLog

| where DeviceVendor has "Check Point"
| where Activity has_any ("Login","Log In","Administrator Login","Authentication","login token") or Message has_any ("SmartConsole","Administrator Login","login token","cpm")
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, Activity, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DeviceAction, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.vendor_product="Check Point*" (Authentication.app="SmartConsole" OR Authentication.app="cpm" OR Authentication.action="success") by Authentication.src Authentication.user Authentication.dest Authentication.action Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | iplocation src | search NOT (src=10.0.0.0/8 OR src=172.16.0.0/12 OR src=192.168.0.0/16) | sort - lastTime
Check Point Management run-script / exec-command on Security Gateway (CVE-2026-62144) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Check Point management audit logs for the run-script and exec-command administrative operations — the exact API commands CVE-2026-62144 lets an unauthenticated attacker invoke to execute arbitrary commands on managed Security Gateways. Any occurrence not tied to an authorized change window is high-signal. Rationale: Uses the literal API command names 'run-script' and 'exec-command' the article and Check Point sk185152 name as the CVE-2026-62144 exploitation primitives; these are rarely used interactively so any hit warrants review. Fixed from prior version by removing the non-canonical AdditionalExtensions column and matching on the canonical Message/Activity fields instead. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/check-point-patches-exploited.html • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk185152/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195848/hacking/check-point-patches-actively-exploited-smartconsole-authentication-bypass-flaw.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized administrator using run-script for legitimate gateway automation/patching
  • Check Point automation/orchestration tooling (Ansible, mgmt_cli scripts) issuing exec-command during maintenance
  • Support/TAC session running diagnostic scripts on a gateway
  • Scheduled config-management job that pushes scripts to gateways
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("svc-cp-automation","ansible-cp") // exclude sanctioned automation service accounts running scripted gateway management
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the administrator/session and SourceIP that issued the run-script/exec-command, and confirm whether it maps to an approved change ticket or automation service account. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the affected gateway from management, revoke the session/credentials, and inspect the gateway for attacker-dropped files or config changes. 3) Hunt: correlate with the IOC IPs, external-source admin logins, and policy installs; review the executed script/command body in the audit record for persistence or defense-evasion actions.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Check Point"
| where Activity has_any ("run-script","exec-command") or Message has_any ("run-script","exec-command")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, Activity, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DeviceAction, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

CVE-2026-62145 Gaia Portal read-only user executing commands as root AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Check Point Gaia telemetry for command execution running with root/expert privileges attributed to a Gaia Portal account holding only read-only privileges — the improper-privilege-management condition CVE-2026-62145 exploits for local privilege escalation on the appliance. Rationale: Targets the article-specific CVE-2026-62145 primitive: a read-only Gaia Portal user reaching root/expert-level command execution, keyed on Gaia Portal audit context plus root/expert/clish/uid=0 markers. Corroborated against Check Point sk185152. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/check-point-patches-exploited.html • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk185152/
ATT&CKT1548 T1068
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Full-admin Gaia operator legitimately entering expert mode for maintenance (not a read-only account)
  • Check Point TAC diagnostics session dropping to expert shell
  • Backup/monitoring integration that runs clish commands under a service account
  • Firmware upgrade or hotfix install invoking root-level scripts
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("admin","cp-maintenance") // exclude accounts that legitimately hold full/expert Gaia privileges
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the Gaia account and confirm its assigned role — if it is a read-only Gaia Portal user reaching root/expert, treat as confirmed escalation. 2) Contain: disable the account, force expert-password rotation, and restrict Gaia Portal access to trusted subnets. 3) Hunt: review the appliance for new local accounts, cron/persistence entries, and correlate with management-plane run-script/exec-command and the IOC IPs.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Check Point"
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("Gaia","Portal") or Message has "Gaia Portal"
| where Message has_any ("uid=0","expert","root","clish") or Activity has_any ("expert","root")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, Activity, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DeviceAction, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Post-exploitation Check Point firewall policy / rule modification from campaign source AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Check Point management audit logs for security-policy and rulebase changes (rule add/delete, policy install) originating from the published IOC source IPs — the 'modify security policies and configurations' impact the article states follows successful CVE-2026-16232 exploitation. Rationale: Combines the concrete IOC source IPs with Check Point policy/rulebase change operations to flag exactly the 'modify security policies and security configurations' impact CVE.org attributes to CVE-2026-16232 — the IOC constraint keeps FPs low. Corroborated against Check Point sk185152 and Help Net Security. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/check-point-patches-exploited.html • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk185152/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/check-point-vulnerability-cve-2026-16232/
ATT&CKT1562 T1531 T1565
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate emergency policy push during the same window as a false-positive IOC hit
  • Reused public IP now belonging to a sanctioned MSP performing policy changes
  • NAT/proxy presenting a public IP for internal admins making routine rulebase edits
  • Automated policy-compliance tool installing policy from a cloud egress IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full changed-rule/object diff for the flagged policy operation and confirm the administrator identity and SourceIP against approved changes and the IOC list. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, revert to the last known-good policy revision, revoke the acting admin session, and restrict Trusted Clients / firewall the management interface. 3) Hunt: enumerate all changes made in that session (new access-roles, any-any rules, disabled protections), check for new administrator accounts, and correlate with run-script/exec-command activity.

| where SourceIP in ("151.241.99.207","151.241.99.233","158.62.198.182","192.142.10.99","139.28.37.250","194.213.18.137") or not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, Activity, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DeviceAction, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

New Check Point administrator account created from external / IOC source (post-compromise persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts Check Point management audit logs for creation of new administrator accounts or admin-privilege grants originating from a public or IOC source IP — a persistence step available once CVE-2026-16232/62144 grant full admin access to the management server. Rationale: Flags administrator-account creation on the Check Point management server from a public or IOC source IP — the natural persistence action after the article's 'full administrative privileges' compromise. The external/IOC source constraint keeps it tied to the campaign rather than routine admin provisioning. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/check-point-patches-exploited.html • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk185152/ • https://www.securityweek.com/new-check-point-zero-day-vulnerability-exploited-in-the-wild/
ATT&CKT1136 T1098 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Onboarding a new admin during a legitimately internet-facing management deployment
  • MSP creating a delegated admin account from their public egress
  • IdP/SSO integration provisioning a management account via an external connector
  • Break-glass account creation during an incident from an out-of-band public IP
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("identity-provisioning-svc") // exclude sanctioned automated admin-provisioning integrations
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the newly created administrator object, the acting admin, and the SourceIP; verify against change tickets and the IOC list. 2) Contain: disable/delete the unauthorized administrator, revoke its sessions and API keys, and enforce Trusted-Client restrictions on management. 3) Hunt: review that account's subsequent actions (policy installs, run-script/exec-command), enumerate all admins for other unexpected additions, and correlate with the campaign IOC IPs.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
