Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663

SQL injection isn't dead

Aikido
2026-07-22 4 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

The fix for SQL injection is decades old and still works. So why did WordPress core just need an emergency patch for one? The data, and how to defend against it. Category: News

CVEsCVE-2026-60137 CVE-2026-63030 CVE-2024-42005
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] wp2shell SQLi via author__not_in REST parameter (CVE-2026-60137) · [LLM] WordPress web-server/PHP process spawning a shell (wp2shell RCE)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious PHP plugin/webshell dropped in wp-content by web server (wp2shell)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
wp2shell SQLi via author__not_in REST parameter (CVE-2026-60137) AIExploitation High
Hunts WordPress REST requests where the author__not_in parameter (normally an integer ID array) carries SQL-injection content, the core signature of CVE-2026-60137 exploited through the batch-route desync in the wp2shell chain. Targets the initial unauthenticated exploitation step against /wp-json/wp/v2/posts. Rationale: author__not_in is documented (Rapid7/VulnCheck) to accept only integer author IDs; any SQL metacharacter in it is the CVE-2026-60137 injection signature. Note: PoCs delivered inside a POST /wp-json/batch/v1 body won't appear in access-log query strings — pair with WAF body inspection (CommonSecurityLog RequestURL/DeviceCustomString) to catch batch-wrapped payloads. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: WordPress web-request telemetry does not live in EDR/CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.tenable.com/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137-frequently-asked-questions-about-remote-code-execution • https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/wp2shell • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/wp2shell-millions-wordpress-sites-remote-takeover
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (WPScan, Nessus, Qualys) sending SQLi test strings to /wp-json/wp/v2/posts
  • Security researchers / bug-bounty testers replaying the public wp2shell PoC against your own estate
  • Legitimate REST clients that URL-encode a comma-separated author list where an ID happens to contain a matched token (rare)
  • WAF-decoded double requests logging both the encoded and decoded query, doubling alert volume
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has_any ("WPScan","Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","sqlmap") and cIP !in ("<your_scanner_ips>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull all requests from the source IP; confirm author__not_in carries SQL (quotes, UNION, SLEEP, information_schema) rather than integers, and note HTTP status — a 200 on a time-based/UNION probe indicates successful injection. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the WAF/edge and confirm the site is on WordPress 7.0.2 / 6.9.5 / 6.8.6; if unpatched, force the emergency update immediately (WordPress.org enabled forced auto-updates for this). 3) HUNT: Pivot to the same host for post-exploit activity — new administrator accounts, PHP files written under wp-content/plugins or wp-content/uploads, and web-server/PHP processes spawning shells (see companion UCs).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "wp-json" or csUriQuery has "rest_route"
| where csUriQuery has "author__not_in"
| where csUriQuery has_any ("'","%27","union","select","sleep","information_schema","0x","--","/*")
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, Computer
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WordPress wp2shell SQL Injection via author__not_in Parameter (CVE-2026-60137)
id: 8f2c1a44-3e5d-4b6a-9c2f-1a7b9d0e4c11
description: Detects SQL-injection content in the WordPress REST author__not_in parameter, which normally only accepts integer post-author IDs. Core signature of the wp2shell pre-auth RCE chain.
references:
  - https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/
  - https://www.tenable.com/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137-frequently-asked-questions-about-remote-code-execution

  - attack.initial_access

  selection_param:

  selection_sqli:

      - '%27'
      - 'union'

      - 'information_schema'
      - '0x'
      - '--'
      - '/*'
  condition: selection_param and selection_sqli

  - Security scanners (Nessus, Qualys, WPScan) probing the endpoint
level: high
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.status) as status values(Web.http_method) as http_method from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*author__not_in*" AND (Web.url="*'*" OR Web.url="*%27*" OR Web.url="*union*" OR Web.url="*UNION*" OR Web.url="*select*" OR Web.url="*SELECT*" OR Web.url="*sleep*" OR Web.url="*information_schema*" OR Web.url="*0x*" OR Web.url="*--*" OR Web.url="*/*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_user_agent Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - lastTime
WordPress web-server/PHP process spawning a shell (wp2shell RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects the code-execution stage of wp2shell where the web-request handler (php-fpm, php-cgi, w3wp, apache/nginx) spawns a command shell or download utility — behaviour a normal WordPress worker never exhibits. Confirms the SQLi chain has reached remote code execution. Rationale: The wp2shell chain culminates in uploading a malicious plugin for code execution; that code runs under the PHP/web-server process, so a web worker spawning cmd/sh/whoami/curl is a direct RCE confirmation. Datadog uses windows.sysmon (IIS/PHP-on-Windows); Linux hosts should use source:linux.auditd EXECVE with the same process names. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/ • https://cyberinsider.com/wordpress-releases-emergency-update-for-critical-wp2shell-rce-flaw/ • https://www.indusface.com/blog/wp2shell-wordpress-cve-2026-60137-63030-rce/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup plugins (UpdraftPlus, BackWPup) shelling out to mysqldump/gzip/tar
  • Image-optimisation plugins invoking imagemagick 'convert' or 'jpegoptim' via PHP exec()
  • wp-cron running PHP CLI jobs that legitimately call curl to fetch feed data
  • Server-monitoring agents that fork sh from the PHP-FPM pool for health checks
  • Composer/WP-CLI maintenance run interactively on the web host by an admin
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mysqldump","imagemagick","convert","jpegoptim","wp-cron.php","backwpup","updraft"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — reconnaissance (whoami, id, uname), outbound fetch (curl/wget to an unknown host), or an interactive shell are strong TP signals; confirm the parent PHP worker is serving the WordPress vhost. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and rotate WordPress DB and admin credentials; take a forensic copy of wp-content before remediation. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all administrator accounts for rogue additions, list recently-modified PHP files under wp-content/plugins and wp-content/uploads, and review web logs for the preceding author__not_in / batch/v1 exploitation requests.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","httpd","apache2","nginx.exe","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","whoami.exe","whoami","curl.exe","curl","wget","python.exe","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-cgi","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","/sh","/bash","/dash","whoami","curl","wget","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WordPress Web-Server/PHP Process Spawning Shell (wp2shell RCE)
id: 2b9e5c17-6d41-4a8e-b3c0-7f21a9e4d502
description: Web-request handler (php-fpm/php-cgi/w3wp/apache/nginx) spawning a command interpreter or download tool, indicating web-shell command execution from the wp2shell chain.

Malicious PHP plugin/webshell dropped in wp-content by web server (wp2shell) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts PHP files written into wp-content/plugins or wp-content/uploads by the web-server/PHP process — the persistence/execution payload the wp2shell chain uploads after minting a rogue admin. Distinguishes attacker-dropped web shells from normal user-initiated plugin installs by anchoring on the writing process and target path. Rationale: The documented wp2shell escalation uploads a malicious plugin for code execution; a PHP file written into wp-content/plugins or the uploads dir by the PHP/web-server process is the on-disk artefact of that step. Anchored on both the target path and writing process to separate attacker drops from normal user-driven plugin installs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/wp2shell • https://www.tenable.com/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137-frequently-asked-questions-about-remote-code-execution
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1505
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator installing or updating a legitimate plugin from the WordPress dashboard (writes many .php files to wp-content/plugins)
  • Automatic plugin/theme auto-updates writing PHP during maintenance windows
  • Caching plugins (W3 Total Cache, WP Rocket) generating advanced-cache.php or object-cache.php
  • Media/gallery plugins writing helper PHP into wp-content/uploads
  • WP-CLI 'wp plugin install' run by an operator on the host
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp plugin install","wp plugin update","advanced-cache.php","object-cache.php") or FolderPath has_any ("w3-total-cache","wp-rocket"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the dropped PHP — short obfuscated files or those containing eval/base64_decode/system/assert/$_POST[ are web shells; a single .php landing directly in wp-content/uploads is almost never legitimate. Check whether the write coincides with a dashboard plugin install by a known admin. 2) CONTAIN: Quarantine the file, hash and submit it, and isolate the host if it is a web shell; revoke sessions and reset admin/DB credentials. 3) HUNT: Correlate the write time backward to author__not_in/batch/v1 exploitation in web logs and forward to web-server processes spawning shells or outbound C2, and audit wp_users for a rogue administrator created just before the drop.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "wp-content" and (FolderPath has "plugins" or FolderPath has "uploads")
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","httpd","nginx.exe","nginx","apache2")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has "wp-content" and (TargetFilePath has "plugins" or TargetFilePath has "uploads")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-cgi","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Adobe Acrobat Extension Flaw Let Malicious Sites Read WhatsApp Web Data

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputer
2026-07-22 14 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched vulnerability chain in the Adobe Acrobat Chrome extension that has over 314 million users, which, if exploited, could facilitate a silent hijack of a user's WhatsApp data. The shortcoming has been codenamed HermeticReader by Guardio Labs. It's officially tracked as CVE-2026-48294 (CVSS score: 7.4), with the vulnerability

CVEsCVE-2026-48294
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1539 T1555.003 T1566
Domainswww.attackers-page.com www.google.attacker.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable Adobe Acrobat Chrome extension (HermeticReader / CVE-2026-48294) present on endpoints · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] First-ever WhatsApp Web contact from a browser on a HermeticReader-vulnerable host · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Vulnerable Adobe Acrobat Chrome extension (HermeticReader / CVE-2026-48294) present on endpoints AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces endpoints running the Adobe Acrobat PDF Chrome/Edge extension (ID efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj) at a version at or below 26.5.2.2, which is exploitable by the HermeticReader UXSS chain to silently read WhatsApp Web data. Parses the version segment from the on-disk extension folder and gates on the vulnerable range (fixed build is 26.5.2.3). This is an exposure hunt, not a compromise signal — the exploit itself runs entirely in the browser renderer and leaves no host telemetry. Rationale: Anchored on the concrete extension ID efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj and the vulnerable version ceiling 26.5.2.2 (fixed 26.5.2.3), both cross-confirmed against BleepingComputer, Guardio Labs and NVD. The on-disk extension path + version parse is the only reliable, no-placeholder way to size org exposure since the UXSS exploit itself is renderer-internal and unlogged. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/adobe-chrome-extension-flaw-let-sites-access-private-whatsapp-chats/ • https://guard.io/labs/hermeticreader---the-vulnerability-that-turned-adobe-300m-install-extension-into-a-full-whatsapp-takeover • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48294 • https://helpx.adobe.com/security/products/acrobat/apsb26-43.html
ATT&CKT1176.001 T1203 T1185
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoints where Chrome auto-update already delivered 26.5.2.3 but a stale 26.5.2.2 folder lingers on disk before cleanup
  • Managed/GPO-pinned extension deployments intentionally holding an older build
  • Roaming user profiles replicating an old extension folder to a new host
  • Chrome/Edge profiles under \Extensions\ that were copied for forensic imaging
  • Version string parse failing on non-standard channels (Beta/Dev) leaving ExtVersion empty (already filtered out)
Suppression filter
| where Rev != 3 or Build != 2 or Minor != 5 or Major != 26   // exclude the fixed 26.5.2.3 build explicitly
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parsed ExtVersion is truly <=26.5.2.2 and not a leftover folder — check the active version via chrome://extensions or the extension's current manifest.json mtime. 2) Contain: force the extension update to 26.5.2.3 (relaunch browser / push policy ExtensionSettings update_url), or temporarily blocklist the extension ID via browser management policy on high-risk users. 3) Hunt: for confirmed-vulnerable hosts, pivot to UC2 to check whether chrome.exe ever reached web.whatsapp.com in a background/unattended context, and review whether the user handles sensitive WhatsApp Web conversations.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\Extensions\efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj\"
| extend ExtVersion = extract(@"efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj\\([0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+)_", 1, FolderPath)
| where isnotempty(ExtVersion)
| extend v = split(ExtVersion, ".")
| extend Major=toint(v[0]), Minor=toint(v[1]), Build=toint(v[2]), Rev=toint(v[3])
// vulnerable = <= 26.5.2.2 ; fixed build is 26.5.2.3
| where Major < 26 or (Major==26 and (Minor<5 or (Minor==5 and (Build<2 or (Build==2 and Rev<=2)))))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), SamplePath=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, DeviceId, ExtVersion
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Extensions\efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj\"
| extend ExtVersion = extract(@"efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj\\([0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+)_", 1, TargetFilePath)
| where isnotempty(ExtVersion)
| extend v = split(ExtVersion, ".")
| extend Major=toint(v[0]), Minor=toint(v[1]), Build=toint(v[2]), Rev=toint(v[3])
| where Major < 26 or (Major==26 and (Minor<5 or (Minor==5 and (Build<2 or (Build==2 and Rev<=2)))))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), SamplePath=any(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ExtVersion
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\Extensions\\efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj\\* OR *\\extensions\\efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj\\*)

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ExtVersion], function=count())

First-ever WhatsApp Web contact from a browser on a HermeticReader-vulnerable host AIActions on Objectives Low
Composite hunt: a host that carries the vulnerable Adobe Acrobat extension (ID efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj) makes its first-ever connection to web.whatsapp.com from chrome/edge/brave. HermeticReader silently opens WhatsApp Web in a background tab from an attacker page, so a never-before-seen WhatsApp Web contact on an exposed endpoint is a weak-but-specific exploitation signal. Low confidence / high FP by design — treat as a lead, not an alert. Rationale: Uses the exact exploit target web.whatsapp.com plus the vulnerable extension ID as a co-presence gate, per Guardio's description that the extension 'reaches directly into WhatsApp Web' by opening it in a background tab. The extension-present + first-seen baseline is the only way to lift this above generic 'browser talked to WhatsApp' noise; still Low confidence because normal first-time WhatsApp Web use is indistinguishable at the network layer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/adobe-chrome-extension-flaw-let-sites-access-private-whatsapp-chats/ • https://guard.io/labs/hermeticreader---the-vulnerability-that-turned-adobe-300m-install-extension-into-a-full-whatsapp-takeover
ATT&CKT1185 T1005 T1176.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user genuinely logging into WhatsApp Web for the first time on that device
  • Newly imaged/onboarded host where the 30-day baseline hasn't accumulated prior WhatsApp Web traffic
  • Shared/kiosk workstation where a different user opens WhatsApp Web
  • Corporate DNS/proxy resolving web.whatsapp.com for a link-preview or security scanner rather than a real session
  • Browser prefetch or service-worker background refresh touching web.whatsapp.com without an interactive session
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("kiosk-01","shared-lobby-pc")   // exclude known shared/kiosk endpoints where first-seen WhatsApp Web is expected
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged host, confirm the Adobe extension is actually <=26.5.2.2 (UC1) and check whether the WhatsApp Web contact was interactive — look for a visible tab / user-driven navigation vs a background request with no preceding user click. 2) Contain: if unexplained, force the extension to 26.5.2.3 or blocklist the extension ID for that user, and advise the user to log out all WhatsApp Web sessions (WhatsApp > Linked Devices). 3) Hunt: review outbound chrome.exe connections from that host to newly-seen external domains around the same timestamp (potential exfil endpoint), and check whether other exposed hosts show the same first-seen WhatsApp Web pattern within a short window.
let VulnHosts = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FolderPath has @"\Extensions\efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj\"
    | distinct DeviceId;
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where RemoteUrl has "web.whatsapp.com"
    | distinct DeviceId;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "web.whatsapp.com"
| where DeviceId in (VulnHosts)      // host carries the vulnerable Adobe Acrobat extension
| where DeviceId !in (Baseline)      // first time this host has ever reached WhatsApp Web
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Connections=count() by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen desc
let VulnHosts = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetFilePath has @"\Extensions\efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj\"
    | distinct DvcHostname;
let Baseline = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where Url has "web.whatsapp.com" or HttpHostName =~ "web.whatsapp.com"
    | distinct DvcHostname;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Url has "web.whatsapp.com" or HttpHostName =~ "web.whatsapp.com"
| where DvcHostname in (VulnHosts)
| where DvcHostname !in (Baseline)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Connections=count() by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\brave.exe) @DestinationHostname:web.whatsapp.com
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/web\.whatsapp\.com/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName], function=count())

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48294")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48294")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Exposure hunt: internet-infrastructure devices carrying actively-exploited/KEV CVEs from July 2026 InfraTrust Pulse · [LLM] SonicWall SMA1000 pre-auth SSRF + management-console command injection exploitation (CVE-2026-15409/15410) · [LLM] FortiSandbox unauthenticated OS command injection via crafted HTTP (CVE-2026-39808 / CVE-2026-25089)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Exposure hunt: internet-infrastructure devices carrying actively-exploited/KEV CVEs from July 2026 InfraTrust Pulse AIExploitation High
Cross-references the org's software/vulnerability inventory against the exact CVE IDs the InfraTrust report flags as actively exploited or CISA-KEV-listed (SonicWall SMA1000, FortiSandbox, Qualcomm GPU driver). Surfaces edge/firmware assets still exposed during the active-exploitation window, directly implementing the report's 'patch these first' and 'firmware patch-lag' thesis. Rationale: Uses the five concrete CVE IDs named in the article (SonicWall SMA1000 15409/15410 CVSS 10.0, FortiSandbox 39808/25089 KEV-listed, Qualcomm GPU driver 21385). Exact-match on CVE ID = zero false positives; the point is closing the exploitation window the report warns about, especially firmware assets that patch late. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/16/cisa-adds-three-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410-sonicwall-sma-1000-zero-day-vulnerabilities-exploited-in-the
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM reports a CVE against a device already patched but not yet re-scanned (stale inventory)
  • Appliance firmware CVEs (SonicWall/FortiSandbox) not covered by MDE agents so only Qualcomm/Windows-side hits appear — coverage gap, not FP
  • A device flagged for CVE-2026-21385 that ships a mitigated Qualcomm driver variant
  • Duplicate rows across SoftwareName variants for the same host
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm the SoftwareVersion is genuinely below the fixed build (FortiSandbox fixed 4.4.9/5.0.6) and the device is internet-reachable. 2) Contain: for actively-exploited edge devices (SonicWall SMA1000, FortiSandbox) restrict management-interface exposure and prioritize emergency patch per CISA BOD 26-04 (deadline 2026-07-19). 3) Hunt: on any still-exposed appliance pivot to the SonicWall/FortiSandbox exploitation UCs below and review appliance auth/admin logs for the exploitation window (SonicWall intrusions began 2026-06-22).

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

SonicWall SMA1000 pre-auth SSRF + management-console command injection exploitation (CVE-2026-15409/15410) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP/S to SonicWall SMA1000 remote-access appliances for the exploited chain: pre-auth SSRF against the Appliance Work Place interface (CVE-2026-15409) followed by OS command injection in the Appliance Management Console (CVE-2026-15410). Runs on WAF/proxy/firewall CEF logging in front of the appliance since the appliance itself carries no EDR agent. Rationale: Grounded in corroborated mechanics: CVE-2026-15409 = pre-auth SSRF in the SMA1000 Appliance Work Place interface, CVE-2026-15410 = OS command injection in the Appliance Management Console (Rapid7/Tenable). Anchored to SonicWall device logs + the specific interface paths + shell metacharacters; appliance has no MDE agent so Defender is intentionally blank. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-rapid7-mdr-team-discovers-new-sonicwall-sma1000-zero-days-being-actively-exploited-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/ • https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410-sonicwall-sma-1000-zero-day-vulnerabilities-exploited-in-the • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/21/sonicwall-sma-zero-days-exploited-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SMA1000 admin API automation that URL-encodes reserved characters (%3B/%7C) in parameters
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) probing the appliance from an authorized scanning range
  • SSL-VPN client bookmark/portal requests containing pipe or semicolon in query strings
  • WAF products logging their own blocked-request test payloads
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Rapid7","Nuclei") or SourceIP in ("10.","192.168."))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SourceIP is external/untrusted and the request actually reached the appliance (2xx/3xx vs WAF block); pull the full RequestURL and any following management-console requests from the same SourceIP. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the perimeter, restrict SMA1000 management/Work Place interface to admin VLAN only, and force a config + admin-credential review (attackers sought cached credentials). 3) Hunt: review appliance logs back to 2026-06-22 (reported intrusion start), look for new/rogue admin sessions, unexpected outbound connections from the appliance (custom-malware C2), and cross-check the exposure-hunt UC for unpatched SMA1000 assets.
CommonSecurityLog

| where DeviceVendor has "SonicWall" or DestinationHostName has_any ("sma","workplace","sslvpn")
| where RequestMethod in~ ("POST","PUT") or RequestURL has_any ("cgi-bin","__api__","workplace","management")
| where RequestURL has_any (";","|","`","$(","%60","%3B","%7C","%24%28")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DeviceProduct, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FortiSandbox unauthenticated OS command injection via crafted HTTP (CVE-2026-39808 / CVE-2026-25089) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP/S to FortiSandbox appliances for the crafted-request OS command injection CISA added to KEV on 2026-07-16 (BOD 26-04, deadline 2026-07-19). Detects shell metacharacters in requests to the FortiSandbox management surface. Runs on WAF/proxy/firewall CEF in front of the appliance (no EDR agent on the device). Rationale: Grounded in the corroborated mechanic (both CVEs = unauthenticated OS command injection via specially crafted HTTP requests; affected FortiSandbox 4.2.x/4.4.0-4.4.8/5.0.0-5.0.5, fixed 4.4.9/5.0.6). Anchored to the FortiSandbox host + shell metacharacters in the request; appliance has no MDE agent so Defender is intentionally blank. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/16/cisa-adds-three-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/07/17/attackers-target-critical-fortisandbox-flaws-as-cisa-issues-patch-order/5274287 • https://gbhackers.com/cisa-warns-of-two-fortinet-fortisandbox-flaws/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) firing command-injection test payloads at the FortiSandbox interface
  • Legitimate FortiSandbox API automation URL-encoding reserved characters in job/sample parameters
  • Security team validation of the CVE-2026-39808/25089 patch with a benign PoC
  • Analyst submissions to FortiSandbox whose filenames legitimately contain semicolons or ampersands
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus","Nuclei","Qualys","Rapid7") or SourceIP startswith "10." or SourceIP startswith "192.168.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FortiSandbox build is unpatched (below 4.4.9/5.0.6), the SourceIP is external, and whether the crafted request returned a 200; extract the injected command substring from RequestURL. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP, remove the FortiSandbox management interface from internet exposure, and expedite upgrade to 4.4.9/5.0.6 per BOD 26-04. 3) Hunt: review FortiSandbox for new cron/service entries, unexpected outbound connections, and file writes to web-accessible paths; correlate the same SourceIP against the SonicWall SMA1000 UC and other edge appliances.

Hackers Exploit Windmill Flaw to Read Arbitrary Server Files Without Authentication

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputer
2026-07-22 15 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A high-severity security flaw impacting open-source developer platform Windmill has come under active exploitation in the wild, per VulnCheck. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-29059 (CVSS score: 7.5), a case of unauthenticated path traversal impacting Windmill's "get_log_file" endpoint ("/api/w/{workspace}/jobs_u/get_log_file/{filename}"). "The filename parameter is concatenated into

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Windmill get_log_file unauthenticated path traversal exploitation (CVE-2026-29059) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Exploit Windmill Flaw to Read Arbitrary Server Files Without Authenticat
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Windmill traversal reads /etc/passwd or /proc/1/environ (SUPERADMIN_SECRET theft) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Windmill get_log_file unauthenticated path traversal exploitation (CVE-2026-29059) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to Windmill's /api/w/{workspace}/jobs_u/get_log_file/{filename} endpoint that carry directory-traversal sequences in the filename segment. This is the exact exploitation primitive for CVE-2026-29059, which VulnCheck reports under active exploitation against ~170 exposed instances. Rationale: Anchored on the exact vulnerable endpoint path 'jobs_u/get_log_file' plus traversal tokens (../, %2e%2e, double-encoded %252e) named in the Windmill advisory and VulnCheck reporting — the combination is not something a legitimate Windmill log-download request would ever contain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29059/ • https://github.com/windmill-labs/windmill/security/advisories/GHSA-24fr-44f8-fqwg • https://github.com/Chocapikk/Windfall
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nuclei/Nessus/Qualys) probing the CVE-2026-29059 template
  • DAST tooling in CI/CD hitting a staging Windmill instance
  • Red-team / pentest engagement against the Windmill host
  • Legitimate log filenames that legitimately contain double-dot substrings (rare; would not resolve outside the log dir)
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in (dynamic(["<approved_scanner_ips_reference_list>"])) // maintain as a Sentinel watchlist of sanctioned scanner IPs; keep unknown sources in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP to this Windmill host; inspect the exact traversal target and the HTTP response code/size to judge whether a file was actually returned (200/206 + non-trivial body = successful read). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge and confirm the Windmill instance is upgraded to 1.603.3+; if not, take it off the internet and patch. 3) Hunt: check whether /proc/1/environ or SUPERADMIN_SECRET was read (see the sensitive-file UC), review Windmill for any superadmin job-preview runs from external IPs, and rotate SUPERADMIN_SECRET and any secrets stored on the host.

| where Url has "get_log_file"
| where Url contains ".." or Url contains "%2e%2e" or Url contains "%2E%2E" or Url contains "%252e"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Windmill traversal reads /etc/passwd or /proc/1/environ (SUPERADMIN_SECRET theft) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful (200/206) Windmill get_log_file traversal requests whose target is a high-value system file — /etc/passwd or /proc/1/environ. Per the advisory, /proc/1/environ leaks the SUPERADMIN_SECRET env var, and VulnCheck observed in-the-wild extraction of /etc/passwd; a returned body here is confirmed sensitive-file disclosure. A host-side Falcon variant catches the Windmill process opening those files on a monitored Linux server. Rationale: Uses the two files the advisory/VulnCheck name explicitly (/etc/passwd observed in the wild, /proc/1/environ = SUPERADMIN_SECRET leak) plus a 200/206 success filter so it fires on actual disclosure, not just attempts; Falcon variant catches the windmill process opening those paths on a monitored Linux host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29059/ • https://github.com/windmill-labs/windmill/security/advisories/GHSA-24fr-44f8-fqwg
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized scanner confirming the CVE with a benign /etc/passwd read
  • Pentest proof-of-exploitation screenshot capture
  • Backup/monitoring agent legitimately reading /etc/passwd on the host (Falcon variant) — but not via the windmill binary
  • Configuration-management tooling (Ansible/Salt) reading /etc/passwd under a different parent process (Falcon variant)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm a body was returned (HttpResponseBodyBytes > 0 / 200-206) and identify which file leaked — /proc/1/environ implies SUPERADMIN_SECRET exposure, a critical escalation path. 2) Contain: treat SUPERADMIN_SECRET and all host-stored secrets as compromised — rotate them immediately, block the source IP, and patch to Windmill 1.603.3+. 3) Hunt: search Windmill/web logs for subsequent authenticated superadmin job-preview or job-run activity from external IPs (Bearer-token abuse -> RCE), and review the host for new processes, cron entries, or outbound connections after the read.
// Successful Windmill CVE-2026-29059 disclosure of /etc/passwd or /proc/1/environ (SUPERADMIN_SECRET).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "get_log_file"
| where Url contains ".." or Url contains "%2e%2e" or Url contains "%2E%2E"
| where Url has_any ("passwd","environ","shadow") or Url contains "proc/1/environ" or Url contains "etc/passwd" or Url contains "etc%2fpasswd"
| where tostring(HttpStatusCode) in ("200","206")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpResponseBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname, DstIpAddr
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Windmill get_log_file traversal enumeration / mass file-read from single source AIReconnaissance Medium
Aggregates Windmill get_log_file traversal requests per source IP to surface rapid enumeration — an attacker walking many traversal paths (systematic file discovery) rather than a single opportunistic probe. Complements the single-request detections by catching automated exploitation and post-read filesystem sweeping. Rationale: Reuses the CVE-specific get_log_file + traversal signature but pivots on volume/distinct-path count per source, distinguishing an automated exploit chain or systematic file sweep from a single scanner hit; thresholds are commented for tuning. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/Chocapikk/Windfall • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29059/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner running the full CVE test suite (many requests, many paths)
  • DAST/fuzzing job in CI/CD against a staging Windmill
  • Red-team engagement enumerating the filesystem
  • A legitimate log-viewer UI polling many distinct valid log filenames (would lack traversal tokens and be filtered out)
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in (dynamic(["<approved_scanner_ips_reference_list>"])) // Sentinel watchlist of sanctioned scanner/CI egress IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: review SamplePaths for the source IP to gauge intent (system files like /etc, /proc, app configs, .env, SSH keys = malicious sweep) and whether responses succeeded. 2) Contain: block the source IP, confirm Windmill is patched to 1.603.3+, and if unpatched pull the instance off the internet. 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct file successfully returned to that source, treat all as compromised (rotate secrets/keys), and check for follow-on superadmin API use or second-stage host activity.
// Rapid enumeration of Windmill get_log_file traversal paths from one source (CVE-2026-29059 automated exploitation / filesystem sweep).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Url has "get_log_file"
| where Url contains ".." or Url contains "%2e%2e" or Url contains "%2E%2E"
| summarize AttemptCount = count(), DistinctPaths = dcount(Url), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SamplePaths = make_set(Url, 10) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where AttemptCount >= 10 or DistinctPaths >= 5   // >=10 traversal reqs/hr OR >=5 distinct traversal targets = enumeration, not a one-off probe
| sort by AttemptCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(Web.url) as distinct_paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*get_log_file*" AND (Web.url="*..*" OR Web.url="*%2e%2e*") by Web.src Web.dest span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count>=10 OR distinct_paths>=5
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Web.url) as distinct_paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*get_log_file*" AND (Web.url="*..*" OR Web.url="*%2e%2e*") by Web.src Web.dest span=1h

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
