File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c", "5d91563b6acd54468ae282083cf9ee3d2c9b2daa45a8de9cb661c2195b9f6cbf", "8c4e78b1bc0a0923fccc0cd2d7ca06023b6ab15af079e6b19d7d5d2fddc5488d") or SHA1 in~ ("c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c", "5d91563b6acd54468ae282083cf9ee3d2c9b2daa45a8de9cb661c2195b9f6cbf", "8c4e78b1bc0a0923fccc0cd2d7ca06023b6ab15af079e6b19d7d5d2fddc5488d") or MD5 in~ ("c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c", "5d91563b6acd54468ae282083cf9ee3d2c9b2daa45a8de9cb661c2195b9f6cbf", "8c4e78b1bc0a0923fccc0cd2d7ca06023b6ab15af079e6b19d7d5d2fddc5488d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c", "5d91563b6acd54468ae282083cf9ee3d2c9b2daa45a8de9cb661c2195b9f6cbf", "8c4e78b1bc0a0923fccc0cd2d7ca06023b6ab15af079e6b19d7d5d2fddc5488d") or SHA1 in~ ("c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c", "5d91563b6acd54468ae282083cf9ee3d2c9b2daa45a8de9cb661c2195b9f6cbf", "8c4e78b1bc0a0923fccc0cd2d7ca06023b6ab15af079e6b19d7d5d2fddc5488d") or MD5 in~ ("c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c", "5d91563b6acd54468ae282083cf9ee3d2c9b2daa45a8de9cb661c2195b9f6cbf", "8c4e78b1bc0a0923fccc0cd2d7ca06023b6ab15af079e6b19d7d5d2fddc5488d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c", "5d91563b6acd54468ae282083cf9ee3d2c9b2daa45a8de9cb661c2195b9f6cbf", "8c4e78b1bc0a0923fccc0cd2d7ca06023b6ab15af079e6b19d7d5d2fddc5488d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized Newtonsoft.Json Fork Hides Game-Rigging Code in a Working Library

The Hacker News
2026-07-22 16 use cases 9 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a NuGet typosquat that's unlike the typical information-stealing malware distributed via package registries: usual info-stealers: it's designed to rig live game results on Digitain. The package, named "Newtonsoftt.Json.Net," masquerades as the Newtonsoft.Json library and is a trojanized fork. Seven versions of the package have been published to the

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Trojanized NuGet typosquat 'Newtonsoftt.Json.Net' restored into a .NET build · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Newtonsoftt.Json.Net trojan C2/exfil beacon to 185.126.237.64:5341 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Trojanized NuGet typosquat 'Newtonsoftt.Json.Net' restored into a .NET build AIDelivery High
Hunts for the specific malicious Newtonsoft.Json fork 'Newtonsoftt.Json.Net' (double-t typosquat) being pulled from NuGet and unpacked into a developer or build-server package cache. This is the initial-access foothold for the Digitain FG-Crash game-rigging supply-chain attack; the package name is unique and never appears in a clean environment. Rationale: Uses the exact typosquat package name 'Newtonsoftt.Json.Net' (double-t) called out by JFrog and confirmed by The Hacker News; the name is unique to this campaign so any file-cache write of it is high-fidelity. Corroborated against JFrog's original research. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/trojanized-newtonsoftjson-fork-hides.html • https://jfrog.com/blog/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally downloading the sample for analysis into a sandbox
  • A threat-intel or SOAR enrichment job caching the .nupkg for detonation
  • A blocklist/allowlist automation writing the package name into a report file (matches on path but not a real install)
  • A developer who deliberately references the package while reproducing the advisory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe") and FolderPath !has @"\Sandbox\" and FolderPath !has @"\Quarantine\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the write path is a real package cache (~/.nuget/packages, build agent workspace) versus an analyst sandbox; capture the exact version folder (11.0.4–11.0.11) and the initiating process (dotnet.exe/nuget.exe/msbuild.exe). 2) Contain: quarantine the package folder, purge it from the offending cache/feed, and pin Newtonsoft.Json to a known-good version via packages.lock.json; block downstream builds from restoring it. 3) Hunt: on the same host and any build server that consumed this artifact, pivot to UC2 for outbound connections to 185.126.237.64:5341 to confirm whether the payload detonated on a Digitain FG-Crash backend.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "newtonsoftt.json.net" or FileName startswith "newtonsoftt.json.net"
| where FileName endswith ".nupkg" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FolderPath has @"\.nuget\packages\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "newtonsoftt.json.net" or TargetFileName startswith "newtonsoftt.json.net"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Trojanized NuGet Typosquat Newtonsoftt.Json.Net File Write
id: 3f1c9a52-8d47-4e6b-9b21-4c2a7d5e0f11
description: Detects the malicious double-t typosquat fork Newtonsoftt.Json.Net (Digitain FG-Crash game-rigging supply-chain trojan) being written to a NuGet package cache or build output.

  - https://jfrog.com/blog/

  category: file_event

    TargetFilename|contains: 'newtonsoftt.json.net'

level: high

#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/newtonsoftt\.json\.net/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*newtonsoftt.json.net*" OR Filesystem.file_name="newtonsoftt.json.net*.nupkg") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Newtonsoftt.Json.Net trojan C2/exfil beacon to 185.126.237.64:5341 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for outbound connections to the hard-coded exfiltration endpoint 185.126.237.64 on TCP 5341 used by the Newtonsoftt.Json.Net trojan to ship rigged FG-Crash round results disguised as telemetry. This confirms the payload actually detonated (target-specific), not merely that the package was installed. Rationale: Uses the hard-coded C2/exfil IOC 185.126.237.64:5341 stated in the article and confirmed by JFrog; the unusual high port + fixed IP is high-fidelity. The malware also tags traffic with the custom header 'X-Seq-ApiKey: theperfectheist2025' — add that as a proxy/web-gateway enrichment where full HTTP header logging exists. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/trojanized-newtonsoftjson-fork-hides.html • https://jfrog.com/blog/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel analyst deliberately detonating the sample and beaconing to the sink IP from a sandbox
  • A blue-team purple-team exercise replaying the IOC
  • A honeypot or deception host configured to attract the C2
  • Automated IOC connectivity/health checks that probe known-bad IPs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "honeypot"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (should be a .NET host process that loaded the trojan JSON assembly) and confirm the host previously restored Newtonsoftt.Json.Net (pivot to UC1); capture destination bytes and periodicity. 2) Contain: block 185.126.237.64:5341 at the perimeter firewall/EDR, isolate the host if it is an FG-Crash/Digitain backend, and snapshot memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: search proxy/web-gateway logs for the custom header 'X-Seq-ApiKey: theperfectheist2025', review FG-Crash round-outcome data for statistical manipulation, and sweep all build servers that consumed the package for the same egress.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "185.126.237.64" and RemotePort == 5341
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "185.126.237.64" and DestinationPort == 5341
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

Microsoft Azure DevOps MCP Flaw Lets Hidden PR Comments Hijack AI Review Agents

The Hacker News
2026-07-22 12 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A single invisible comment in an Azure DevOps pull request can turn a reviewer's own AI coding agent against them, driving it into projects the attacker has no rights to reach and quietly leaking what it finds. The flaw is in Microsoft's official Azure DevOps MCP server, and it works because one of its tools returns pull request descriptions without a prompt-injection guardrail the company had

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Azure DevOps MCP server launched without least-privilege domain scope (no -d flag) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Azure DevOps MCP server loaded with abusable pipelines/wiki/security domains in a review context · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Azure DevOps MCP server launched without least-privilege domain scope (no -d flag) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts developer/CI endpoints running Microsoft's official @azure-devops/mcp server with a broad token and NO -d domain restriction, which is the exact posture Manifold Security says concentrates the confused-deputy risk: a hidden PR-description comment can then drive the reviewer's agent across pipelines, wikis, repos and work items it never needed. Article-specific because it keys on the real package name and the -d least-privilege flag Microsoft documents. Rationale: Keys on the confirmed npm package name @azure-devops/mcp and the -d least-privilege flag from Microsoft's own GETTINGSTARTED docs; a broad token with no -d is the precise risk-concentration posture Manifold and THN describe. Cross-checked microsoft/azure-devops-mcp repo docs and the THN write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-azure-devops-mcp-flaw-lets.html • https://github.com/microsoft/azure-devops-mcp/blob/main/docs/GETTINGSTARTED.md • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@azure-devops/mcp
ATT&CKT1204 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevOps engineer intentionally running the full-scope MCP server for general Azure DevOps automation (not code review) where broad tooling is acceptable
  • Self-hosted Azure Pipelines build agent (Agent.Worker.exe/Agent.Listener.exe) launching the server with a service PAT for CI tasks
  • Initial one-time setup/testing of the MCP server before an operator adds -d scoping
  • Solo/hobby repos with no external contributors, where an over-scoped token carries no real confused-deputy exposure
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("agent.worker.exe", "agent.listener.exe")   // exclude self-hosted Azure Pipelines build agents running the server for CI
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the token/PAT scope the server was started with and whether the same host runs a coding agent (Copilot CLI, Claude Code, node) in an auto-approve posture with no per-tool prompts. 2) Contain: re-launch the server with `-d` limited to the domains the task needs (e.g. `-d core repositories work-items`) and drop pipelines/wiki/comment-posting from any code-review tool set; downscope the PAT to the project under review and enable per-tool approval. 3) Hunt: pull Azure DevOps audit logs for cross-project pipeline runs, wiki reads, or PR comments posted by this user during reviews, and scan open PR descriptions for hidden HTML comments (`<!-- ... -->`) that could carry an injection payload.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@azure-devops/mcp"
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has "-d")   // -d flag = per-domain least-privilege scoping; absence loads ALL domains
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          Agent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          Runtime = FileName,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "@azure-devops/mcp"
| where not(CommandLine has "-d")   // no per-domain restriction = broad token, full tool surface
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Azure DevOps MCP Server Launched Without Least-Privilege Domain Scope
id: 7463d74f-5fd7-4d25-afee-bc9ca57cbd59
status: experimental
description: Detects the official @azure-devops/mcp server started without the -d domain flag, exposing the full pipelines/wiki/repos/work-items tool surface an injected PR comment can abuse.

  - https://github.com/microsoft/azure-devops-mcp/blob/main/docs/GETTINGSTARTED.md
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/22

  product: windows

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/@azure-devops\/mcp/i

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Azure DevOps MCP server loaded with abusable pipelines/wiki/security domains in a review context AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts endpoints where @azure-devops/mcp is explicitly scoped (via -d) to include the pipelines, wiki, or advanced-security domains — the exact tools Manifold's PoC chained (trigger a pipeline in another project, read a confidential wiki, post it back as a PR comment). A code-review tool set has no legitimate need for these, so their presence is the abusable surface. Distinct pivot from UC1: positive match on the loaded-domain tokens rather than absence of -d. Rationale: Positively matches the pipelines/wiki/advanced-security domain tokens that Manifold's PoC chain actually exercised (pipeline trigger -> confidential wiki read -> PR-comment exfil), grounded in the real -d domain names from Microsoft's docs. Cross-checked the microsoft/azure-devops-mcp docs and THN article. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-azure-devops-mcp-flaw-lets.html • https://github.com/microsoft/azure-devops-mcp/blob/main/docs/GETTINGSTARTED.md
ATT&CKT1213 T1204
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate release/pipeline automation where the operator genuinely needs the pipelines domain and there is no untrusted-PR review workflow
  • Documentation or wiki-maintenance agents that intentionally load the wiki domain
  • Security teams using the advanced-security domain for CodeQL/alert triage rather than PR review
  • One-off broad-scope invocation by a DevOps engineer exploring MCP tooling
  • Full-scope launches with no -d at all that also happen to log these domain names via server startup banners (validate the token appears as a CLI arg, not stdout)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("agent.worker.exe", "agent.listener.exe")   // exclude self-hosted Azure Pipelines build agents
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify whether this host runs an interactive code-review agent and whether the loaded pipelines/wiki/advanced-security domains are actually required for that workflow; confirm auto-approve (no per-tool prompt) posture. 2) Contain: re-scope the server to only the domains the task needs and strip pipeline-run, wiki-read, and comment-post tools from the review tool set; require per-tool approval so an odd cross-project pipeline run is caught before it fires. 3) Hunt: in Azure DevOps audit logs, correlate this user/PAT for a pipeline run in one project plus a wiki read plus a PR comment within the same review window (the PoC signature), and grep recent PR descriptions for hidden `<!-- -->` HTML comments.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@azure-devops/mcp"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pipelines", "wiki", "advanced-security")   // domains abused in Manifold PoC; not needed by a code-review agent
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          Agent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "@azure-devops/mcp"
| where CommandLine has_any ("pipelines", "wiki", "advanced-security")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-16232")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-16232")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Gitea vulnerable PR-update API route access (CVE-2026-58443 public-only token bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP POST requests to Gitea's pull-request update endpoint POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/update, the exact route CVE-2026-58443 abuses so a public-only,write:repository token pushes public base commits into a PRIVATE head branch. Article-specific because the route path, method, and behaviour are the vulnerability signature; correlate the captured source IP / authenticated principal against token scope in Gitea's own admin/audit view to confirm exploitation. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable route from the advisory (POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/update) plus HTTP method — the concrete CVE-2026-58443 signature. Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: none of those telemetry sets ship Gitea reverse-proxy request paths+methods; token-scope-vs-target-repo correlation must be finished in Gitea's own audit log. Corroborated fixed version (1.27.0) and route via GitLab advisory and multiple vendor write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xxjv-752h-3vp2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58443/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gitea-vulnerability/ • https://securityonline.info/gitea-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate maintainers clicking the Gitea 'Update branch' button (calls the same API route)
  • CI/CD service accounts programmatically syncing PR branches with the base branch
  • Automated merge/rebase bots (e.g. renovate/dependabot-style) that update PRs
  • Repository owners updating their own private-repo PRs via a fully-scoped token
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, pull the source IP and authenticated principal from the Gitea admin panel; in Gitea, check whether the token used carried the public-only scope and whether the PR's HEAD repository is PRIVATE while the base (route) repo is public — that combination is the exploit, a same-owner fully-scoped update is benign. 2) Contain: revoke and rotate the offending token, and upgrade Gitea to 1.27.0 (patch #38406); temporarily restrict PR-update to authenticated maintainers if patching is delayed. 3) Hunt: enumerate Actions workflow runs in the affected private repo around the event time (the malicious push can trigger private CI), review git push events into private head branches attributable to that token, and check for secrets exfil in those workflow logs.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)/api/v1/repos/[^/]+/[^/]+/pulls/[0-9]+/update"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Gitea instance exposed to CVE-2026-58443 (version <= 1.26.4) AIExploitation High
Surfaces managed hosts running a Gitea build vulnerable to CVE-2026-58443 (all releases up to and including 1.26.4; fixed in 1.27.0) so exposure can be remediated before the public-token-to-private-repo bypass is exploited. Article-specific via the exact CVE identifier and affected product. Rationale: Keys on the concrete CVE-2026-58443 identifier and the Gitea product name; affected-range (<=1.26.4) and fix (1.27.0) confirmed against the GitLab advisory mirror and multiple vendor write-ups. Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty as vuln-state exposure is not carried in FDR/CloudTrail/Datadog log telemetry here. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58443/ • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.27.0/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gitea-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched to 1.27.0 but scanner catalog not yet refreshed (stale finding)
  • Air-gapped/internal-only Gitea with no untrusted token issuance (real but low-risk exposure)
  • Custom/forked Gitea build whose version banner mis-maps to the CVE
  • Container image tag pinned <=1.26.4 in a non-production sandbox
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is truly <= 1.26.4 and that the instance issues API tokens to users beyond trusted admins (public-only tokens are the attack precondition). 2) Contain: schedule/apply the upgrade to Gitea 1.27.0 (patch #38406); until patched, audit and where possible revoke public-only,write:repository tokens and restrict PR-update on public base repos. 3) Hunt: pivot to the CVE-2026-58443 web-route detection for this host to see if the vulnerable endpoint was already exercised, and review recent private-repo Actions workflow triggers.
